extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics students, and philosophers of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing philosophies of mathematics, foundations, proofs, and mathematical practice — e.g., formalism, constructivism, Lakatosian fallibilism — and for judging what counts as acceptable proof, explanation, or foundation. Focuses on both formal/metamathematical requirements and informal/practical standards used by working mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational certitude / consistency requirement (Hilbert)
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal of a foundational program is to establish once and for all the certitude of mathematical methods; mathematics should be shown consistent so that its methods are indubitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert’s program sought a metamathematical justification (prove consistency of mathematics within a finitary framework). Gödel’s incompleteness theorems show this ideal is unattainable for sufficiently strong systems, so claims of absolute certitude via formalization are undermined. Use caution when treating consistency proofs as delivering final certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalist definition: mathematics as the science of rigorous proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is defined as the science of rigorous proof: start from undefined terms and axioms and derive theorems by valid logical deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formalist measures mathematical work by its formal deductions from axioms; the logical import of axioms does not depend on mental pictures. This view treats theorems as consequences of axioms (neither true nor false absent interpretation) and values formal rigor above informal content or interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructivist criterion: start from the intuitively given (counting/finite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics must start from the intuitively given, the finite, and contain only what is obtained constructively from this starting point; intuition here means the intuition of counting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brouwer’s intuitionism rejects identifying mathematics with formal formulas and insists on constructive methods. This is a strict constraint on acceptable proofs and constructions (anti-pattern: accepting nonconstructive existence proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation / meaningfulness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements in pure mathematics have no content until supplied with an interpretation; only with an interpretation can statements be true or false in the same sense as statements about reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalist perspective: theorems as syntactic consequences lack intrinsic meaning; applying an interpretation (e.g., geometric distances) furnishes content. When evaluating mathematical claims, state whether you're treating them syntactically or semantically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency suffices over objective truth (formalist stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the formalist, it is enough that a theory is consistent rather than 'true' — different theories (e.g., Euclidean and non-Euclidean geometry) can both be legitimate if each is consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing rival theories, prioritize internal consistency and the freedom to study multiple coherent systems rather than seeking a single objectively true geometric description of physical space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms as arbitrary starting points (premathematical choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematician must start with undefined terms and unproved statements (axioms); questions like 'Why these axioms?' are premathematical and, to the formalist, not central to mathematics itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In formal exposition, choices of vocabulary and axioms may be treated as conventional; however, for practice and pedagogy, their motivations and interpretations often matter (anti-pattern: ignoring why axioms were chosen when context demands it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to finitary/metamathematical methods (Hilbert program strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalization attempts to map set theory and analysis into finite combinatorics (finitistic metamathematics) so that the consistency of the whole rests on finitary principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the strategy Hilbert used to justify infinite mathematics; critics note this merely shifts the foundational question to the reliability of the finitistic principles themselves (the 'last tortoise under the last elephant').

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical/formalist style: avoid imagery, examples, and meta-questions
rubrics_metrics.description: From the formalist viewpoint, pictures, diagrams, mental imagery, examples and questions about choice of axioms or applications are non-mathematical or premathematical and thus should be minimized in texts and courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal exposition prioritizes axioms and proofs; anti-patterns for formalists include extensive use of pictures or applications. In contrast, many practitioners find such exclusions pedagogically harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of accomplishment by amount proved (formal instruction metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the formalist instructional model, how much has been proved (in lectures or texts) is used to measure accomplishment; questions of student understanding are considered non-mathematical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion privileges theorem-proving output over comprehension or application. As an evaluative measure it can miss learning outcomes and conceptual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for examples, applications and concrete mathematics (reaction to formalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: A contrasting modern trend values concrete, applicable mathematics, giving more respect to examples and less strictness in formal exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging expositions or research, consider clarity via examples, applicability, and accessibility to practitioners, not only formal rigor. This is often seen as corrective to excessive formalist abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lakatosian growth: conjectures, proofs, and refutations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics grows by a dialectic of conjecture, proof, and counterexample; 'proof' means explanations and justifications that are themselves subject to criticism and revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mathematical work by its ability to withstand and incorporate criticism: does a proof explain counterexamples, does it get refined under pressure, does the evolving theory become more detailed and accurate? Emphasize historical and dialogic processes over static formal derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local versus global counterexamples (diagnostic tool)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'local counterexample' challenges a particular step in an argument; a 'global counterexample' challenges the conclusion itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction when analyzing failures of proofs/theories: attempt to isolate whether the issue is a fixable local flaw or a refutation of the conjecture as stated, guiding strategies for revision or abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance by 'consensus of the qualified' (real-proof standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Real proofs are established by consensus among qualified mathematicians rather than by mechanical transcription into formal logic; acceptance depends on explanation, communication, and community judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the correctness of proofs, consider community vetting: repeated study, alternative proofs, applications, analogies, and the standing of the result in the field contribute to it becoming 'rock bottom.' Recognize human fallibility and that errors may persist for generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi-empiricist criterion: informal theories as potential falsifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: In a quasi-empiricist view (Lakatos), the potential falsifiers of formalized mathematical theories are informal theories — formal systems are judged by how well they reproduce the informal mathematics we had in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate formal axiomatizations by their fidelity to informal mathematical practice and intuition; be open to revising either the formal system or the informal theory in light of discrepancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamathematical infallibility (editorial critique) — formal derivation in first-order logic
rubrics_metrics.description: First-order logic characterizes validity of inference so that, relative to a characterization of logical terms, valid inference is essentially infallible (editors' critique of Lakatos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a theoretical standard: within metamathematics, derivations can be made formally infallible. But apply caution when transferring this standard to informal, human-checked proofs — infallibility is 'in principle' and may not reflect actual practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between mathematics as deductive structure and as descriptive science
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalists distinguish 'geometry as a deductive structure' (mathematics) from 'geometry as a descriptive science' (description of physical space); only the former is strictly mathematical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a theory, clarify whether you judge it by internal deductive merits (consistency, rigor) or by its descriptive/empirical adequacy. Conflating these can cause category errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid identifying metamathematics with actual mathematical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamathematics (formal models, first-order logic) portray an idealized structure of infallible proofs, but real mathematical practice involves informal proofs, gestalt understanding, and community standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments claiming that formal derivability settles all questions should be tempered: recognize the difference between hypothetical 'in-principle' formal proofs and the fallible, communicative processes by which working mathematicians accept results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical case studies as evidence (Lakatos' method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical, historico-critical case studies (e.g., Euler-Descartes formula and its counterexamples) are a legitimate method for evaluating philosophical claims about how mathematics grows and is corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing about the nature of mathematical justification, use detailed historical reconstructions to show how conjectures were proposed, refuted, patched, and refined. History can reveal practices invisible to purely formal accounts.
